newsitem.title: UK: International LPG stable after recent price crash.
newsitem.headline: International LPG stable after recent price crash.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices were stable or lower this week, although trade remained generally quiet following the recent spectacular price falls, dealers said.
In Europe, a small propane coaster trade at $197.50 a tonne fob UK on Friday -- sharply below the last done -- sent ripples through the market.

The buyer, however, pointed out that the last three openly reported trades in which it had been involved were at $197.50, $320 and $442.50 -- a difference of $122.50 between each deal, and representative of the speed at which the market has fallen.
At this price propane becomes an attractive feedstock for cracking for gasoline production, dealers said.

During the winter both propane and butane have been far too expensive relative to naphtha, the alternative cracking feedstock. But propane's present weakness has brought the price below naphtha -- assessed around $213 a tonne on the ARA barge market on Friday -- and made propane a possible feedstock again.
But the market was divided over whether this was a true indication of the current market or a one-off distressed sale. Some feel that the next coaster is likely to be done at nearer to $220.
While coasters were falling, large cargoes remained stable. An 8,000 tonne cargo was reported traded at $245 a tonne cif Germany this week, following deals at $245 and $235 last Friday.

"There's reasonable support at this price," said a trader. "Most of the length has been cleared out. Propane is going to the Med and there's inland demand in North Sea countries, and now it's settled down in the $240's."

But he added there could still be a rebound if bad weather strikes in late February or early March -- it was still very cold across much of northern Europe -- and this could quickly push prices back up again.
Interest for butane has been much thinner, dealers said, with coasters talked in the mid-$220's a tonne fob NWE and cargoes in the $240's.

In the Mediterranean, the market has also been thin over the week. A small propane lot was reported sold at $300 a tonne cif Italy during the week. There was also a North Sea cargo thought sold at $275 cif Spain, and this was the level the market was assessed at on a cif Lavera basis. This reflected the cif North Sea price plus a freight element, dealers said.
Mediterranean butane was thinly discussed. The only real price indication was Sonatrach's official price of $290 a tonne fob Bethioua.
"Obviously this is too high, but it still exists so we have to use it when considering the spot level," said a trader.
Asian markets were also quiet as traders tried to minimise their purchases and wait for lower prices as the winter recedes.

"Japanese buyers still have small monthly requirements but they're checking spot levels and they won't move quickly," said a trader. He added that Saudi Aramco has not yet released its March loading programme, and pointed out that if there are any delays buyers may have to move more quickly than planned.
Both Korean and Chinese buyers are also acting slowly, amid general uncertainty over where the March Saudi Contract Price (CP) will be set.
"Some say the March CP will be $50 below February, others say $20," said a trader. As a result, he said there was now " a rather frustrated market."

Spot premiums are assessed at CP -$20/-$15 fob Gulf, but Japanese levels are much more uncertain, he said. Most discussion is around March CP + $20/$25 a tonne C+F Japan, but the big question remains where the CP will be set.
